Smooth, adjustable blur with a direction — you can blur a single axis.
Lens blur: a disc of samples shaped like the iris, where bright areas weigh more — this is bokeh, not a smear.
Brings out detail and edges without inventing texture.
A real unsharp mask: original + gain × (original − blurred), with a threshold so grain is not amplified.
Raises brightness and opens or closes contrast around mid grey.
Remaps color: each pixel\'s brightness becomes a position on a rotating rainbow.
The tone curve: fine control of light and of each color channel.
Brightens or darkens like camera exposure: multiplies light without blowing out color.
The negative: every color becomes its opposite, like a badly developed film.
Sets where black starts, where white ends and where the middle sits.
Mixes the R, G and B channels together: swaps, adds and crosses colors.
Makes color more vivid, or takes everything to black and white.
Paints the shadows one color and the highlights another — cinema duotone.
An angle you wire into another parameter\'s expression.
An on/off switch you wire into another parameter\'s expression.
A color you wire into another parameter\'s expression.
An X/Y point you wire into another parameter\'s expression.
A value from 0 to 100 you wire into another parameter\'s expression.
The image vanishes in circles growing from the center with a rippling edge. Animate the progress to turn it into a transition.
Deterministic shake: the layer shakes the same way every time you reopen the project, with separate frequency and axes.
A noise field pushes every pixel. The field evolves over time — smoke, heat, water.
Lens: push, pull, twist, sphere and corner, each with its own radius and point.
A wave crosses the image — horizontal, vertical or diagonal — and can be pinned at the edges.
Two bars, one vertical and one horizontal, scan the image reading from the wrong place. Animate the progress to turn it into a transition.
Digital glitch: the image breaks into sliding blocks, the channels split apart and whole blocks jump out of place.
Broadcast signal: lost bands, slipping sync and constant drift.
Stylised VHS: heavy RGB split, wobble, dirty glow and vignette — the vocabulary of tape at the service of the look.
Real VHS: blur, smeared chroma, tracking instability, tape dropouts, scanlines and color degradation.
Removes the green or blue background and cleans the color spill on the edge.
Removes the black (or the white) from the layer and lets the rest show through.
Glow in two halos, one tight and one wide, each with its own color: the core blows out and the surroundings fill in.
Spreads the light from the bright parts: the glow that comes off the screen.
Light rays coming from a point: the brightness of the highlights spreads in straight lines.
A blade of light crosses the image. With relief, it lights only where the surface faces it.
Damaged film: dust, scratches, flicker, gate weave, burns and splices — each with its own control.
Film grain: crystal at whatever size you want, luma and chroma apart, stronger in the shadows.
Halftone: the image becomes dots, with the grid rotated per channel so the three screens do not fight.
Hologram: the image becomes a projection, with a technical grid, scanlines and interference.
JPEG damage: the blocks, the ringing on edges and color at half resolution. Quality scales all three.
Dilates or erodes what is bright: thickens or thins a cutout and cleans up a one-pixel edge.
Repeats the image in a mosaic until it covers the frame, with optional mirror and phase.
Sorts the pixels of each row by brightness: the image melts into streaks.
Screen scanlines: the line darkens whatever is behind it, with its own height, softness and channel.
Leaves a trail: copies of the image itself delayed in time, with fade.
Locks the frame rate: the image starts moving in steps, like hand-drawn animation.
Each color channel comes from a different instant: red from the frame behind, blue from the frame ahead.
Moves, rotates, scales and changes the layer\'s opacity without losing quality.
